items.prompt: What character must a cell entry start with for the spreadsheet to treat it as a formula?
rubric: Formulas begin with an equals sign in both Excel and Google Sheets.
Symbols like # and & appear in errors and operators but do not start formulas.

items.prompt: Which function adds up all the numbers in a range of cells?

options.label: TOTALIZE
MERGE
COUNT
SUM

rubric: SUM adds the numbers in a range.
COUNT tallies how many numbers there are rather than adding them; the others are not standard functions for this.

items.prompt: In the cell reference `C5`, what do the letter and the number identify?

options.label: Row C and column 5
Column C and value 5
Column C and row 5
Sheet C and page 5

rubric: Letters name columns and numbers name rows, so C5 is column C, row 5.
Swapping row and column is the most common confusion.

items.prompt: Which function counts how many cells in a range contain numbers?

options.label: ROUND
LEN
SUMIF
COUNT

rubric: COUNT counts cells holding numeric values.
SUMIF adds conditionally and LEN measures text length.

items.prompt: Which symbol, placed before a column letter or row number, locks that part of a cell reference?
rubric: The dollar sign makes a reference absolute, as in $A$1.
Other symbols have different roles, such as % for percent.

items.prompt: Which of the following are built-in spreadsheet functions? Select all that apply.

options.label: ADDALL
COUNTIF
TOTALIF
AVERAGE
MAX

rubric: AVERAGE, MAX and COUNTIF are standard functions.
ADDALL and TOTALIF sound plausible but do not exist.

items.prompt: Priya has a table of 500 sales rows with columns for region, product and amount. Her manager wants totals per region and per product, and she wants to avoid writing many formulas by hand. Which feature is designed to summarize a table this way?

options.label: Conditional formatting
Freeze panes
Data validation
Pivot table

rubric: A pivot table groups and summarizes rows by categories.
Conditional formatting, validation and freeze panes change appearance or input rules, not summaries.

items.prompt: The formula `=A1+B1` in C1 is copied down to C2. Why does C2 now contain `=A2+B2`?

options.label: Column letters stay put while row numbers reset to one
Relative references shift by the same offset as the copy
The spreadsheet recalculates every formula using the last row
Copying always rewrites formulas to use the row below

rubric: Relative references move with the copied position.
Distractors invent rules that do not describe relative referencing.

items.prompt: A1 holds 2, A2 holds 4 and A3 holds the text `n/a`. What does `=SUM(A1:A3)` return?

options.label: #VALUE!

rubric: SUM ignores text inside a range and adds 2 + 4 = 6.
Learners expect an error or zero because of the text cell.

items.prompt: How does applying a filter to a table differ from sorting it?

options.label: Filtering changes the cell values, while sorting only moves headings
Filtering deletes rows that do not match, while sorting keeps them
Filtering reorders rows by value, while sorting hides some rows
Filtering hides non-matching rows, while sorting reorders all rows

rubric: A filter temporarily hides rows that fail the condition; sorting changes row order.
Many learners think filtering deletes data.

items.prompt: A cell shows `#DIV/0!`. What does this error most likely mean?

options.label: The column is too narrow to show the result
The formula refers to a sheet that was deleted
The formula contains text where a number is needed
The formula divides by zero or by an empty cell

rubric: #DIV/0! signals division by zero or a blank divisor.
Narrow columns show ####, and deleted references give #REF!.

items.prompt: You want to show how monthly website visits changed across 12 months. Which chart type fits best?

options.label: Scatter of random points
Line chart
Pie chart
Stacked area of names

rubric: Line charts show change over time.
Pie charts show parts of a whole at one moment, not a trend.

items.prompt: Which statements about pivot tables are true? Select all that apply.

options.label: They can total values grouped by a category field
They can be rearranged by dragging fields to new positions
They permanently overwrite the source data with totals
They need every cell in the source typed as text
They only work on a single column of data

rubric: Pivot tables group and total data and can be rearranged by moving fields.
They do not alter source data and need a multi-column table with headers.

items.prompt: Sam enters `=B2*C1` in D2, where C1 holds a tax rate, then copies it down the column. D2 is right, but D3 and below show 0. Which explanation fits what happened?

options.label: Excel only calculates the first row, so later rows need the formula retyped
C1 shifted to C2, C3 and so on, which are empty
The B column values below row 2 were stored as text, so they became zero
Copied formulas keep their results from row 2, so they stay at zero after that

rubric: The relative reference C1 moved down to blank cells, giving 0; it should be $C$1.
Other options blame formatting or copying rather than the shifting reference.

items.prompt: A formula `=B2*$E$1` is copied down from row 2 to row 3. What does the `$` in `$E$1` do?

options.label: It formats the result of the formula as a currency value
It makes the formula recalculate only when E1 is changed
It keeps the reference pointing at E1 when copied
It stops other users from editing cell E1 afterwards

rubric: The `$` makes the reference absolute, so it does not shift when copied.
Distractors confuse `$` with currency formatting or cell protection.

items.prompt: The range A1:A13 holds 10 names and 3 empty cells. Which formula returns 10?

options.label: `=COUNT(A1:A13)`
`=COUNTA(A1:A13)`
`=COUNTBLANK(A1:A13)`

rubric: COUNTA counts non-empty cells, including text.
COUNT counts only numbers, so it returns 0 for names; COUNTBLANK returns 3.

items.prompt: A table has names in column A and scores in column B. You sort only column B, keeping the current selection. Why are the results wrong?

options.label: Sorting a single column deletes the neighbouring column, so the names vanish
The scores move but the names stay put, so names pair with the wrong scores
Sorting turns the numbers into text, so scores are compared by first digit
Sorting only works on text, so the scores get rounded to whole numbers

rubric: Rows must move together; sorting one column breaks the link between related values.
Distractors invent side effects that sorting does not have.

items.prompt: What is the main purpose of a pivot table?

options.label: To turn formulas into fixed values so they stop recalculating
To lock a data table so other editors cannot change its values
To summarise data by grouping and totalling it without altering the source
To reorder the source rows permanently so similar entries sit together

rubric: A pivot table summarises and regroups data, leaving the source rows unchanged.
Distractors confuse it with sorting, protection or paste-as-values.

items.prompt: You have sales totals for each of 12 months and want to show how sales rise and fall over time. Which chart type fits best?

options.label: Pie chart
Doughnut chart
Stacked 3D bar chart
Line chart

rubric: A line chart shows change across ordered time periods.
Pie and doughnut charts show parts of a whole, not trends.

items.prompt: A cell shows 1250 aligned to the left, and `SUM` ignores it. Which could explain this? Select all that apply.

options.label: The number was entered with a leading apostrophe
The cell was formatted as Text before the number was typed
The cell has a yellow fill colour applied
The column is too narrow to show the number

rubric: Text formatting or a leading apostrophe stores the number as text, which SUM skips and which aligns left.
Narrow columns show ##### and fill colour does not change the data type.

items.prompt: Priya types the date 14/03/2025 into a cell. The cell shows `########`, yet the formula bar displays the date correctly. She asks what is wrong. What is the most likely explanation?

options.label: The date is invalid for the sheet's locale, so it replaced the entry with a placeholder
The cell holds a circular reference, so it cannot calculate and show any result
The value is too wide for the column, so widening the column displays it
The date was stored as text, so it must be converted to a true date number

rubric: ######## means the value does not fit the column width; the data itself is fine.
Distractors treat it as a data or formula error.

items.prompt: Cells A1:A5 contain 4, 8, 12, 16 and 20. What does `=AVERAGE(A2:A4)` return?
rubric: A2:A4 holds 8, 12, 16; their mean is 12.
10 and 14 come from using the wrong range.

items.prompt: Cell C2 contains `=A2*B2`. You copy it to C5. What formula appears in C5?
rubric: Relative references shift by the same number of rows, giving A5 and B5.
Other options assume partly or fully fixed references.

items.prompt: B2 holds 62 and C2 holds the text "No". What does `=IF(AND(B2>=50,C2="Yes"),"Pass","Review")` return?

options.label: #VALUE!
Review
Pass
FALSE

rubric: AND needs both conditions true; C2 is "No", so the false branch returns Review.
Choosing Pass ignores the second condition.

items.prompt: A product table sits in A:C (ID, Name, Price). F2 holds an ID. Which formula returns that product's price for an exact ID match?

options.label: `=VLOOKUP(F2,A:C,3,TRUE)`
`=VLOOKUP(F2,A:C,2,FALSE)`
`=VLOOKUP(F2,B:C,3,FALSE)`
`=VLOOKUP(F2,A:C,3,FALSE)`

rubric: Price is the 3rd column of A:C and FALSE forces an exact match.
Index 2 returns the name, TRUE allows approximate match, and B:C has no third column.

items.prompt: Regions are in A2:A20 and sale amounts in B2:B20. Which formula totals the sales for West?

options.label: `=COUNTIF(A2:A20,"West")`
`=SUMIF(B2:B20,"West",A2:A20)`
`=SUM(A2:A20,"West")`
`=SUMIF(A2:A20,"West",B2:B20)`

rubric: SUMIF takes the criteria range, the criterion, then the range to add.
Swapped ranges or COUNTIF give wrong results.

items.prompt: A1 holds 10, A2 holds 20 and A3 holds the text "n/a". Which formulas return 30? Select all that apply.

options.label: `=AVERAGE(A1:A3)*2`

rubric: SUM and AVERAGE ignore text in ranges: SUM gives 30, AVERAGE is 15 so doubled is 30.
Adding with + hits the text and gives #VALUE!; COUNT(...)*10 gives 20.

items.prompt: A sheet has 500 order rows with columns Region, Rep and Sales. Your manager wants the average sale amount for each region. You insert a pivot table. Which setup gives this?

options.label: Rows: Region; Values: Sales, summarised as Average
Rows: Sales; Values: Region, summarised as Count
Columns: Rep; Values: Sales, summarised as Max
Rows: Region; Values: Sales, summarised as Sum

rubric: Group by Region and summarise Sales with Average.
Sum gives totals, not averages; the other setups group by the wrong field.

items.prompt: Region names are in A2:A6 and sale amounts in B2:B6. Which formula totals the amounts for rows where the region is West and the amount is over 100?
rubric: SUMIFS takes the sum range first, then each criteria range followed by its criterion.
Distractors misuse SUMIF with multiple criteria, or omit a criteria range or the sum range.

items.prompt: A tax rate sits in F1. In C2 you need a formula that multiplies B2 by that rate, and it will be filled down to C20 so every row uses F1. Which formula do you enter?
rubric: Anchoring F1 with $F$1 keeps the rate fixed while B2 changes for each row.
Relative F1 drifts to F2, F3 and so on, and anchoring B2 freezes the amount instead.

items.prompt: Product IDs are in column A of the current sheet. The Prices sheet holds IDs in A2:A50 and unit prices in column C. Which formula in B2 returns the exact price for the ID in A2?

options.label: `=VLOOKUP(A2,Prices!A2:C50,3,TRUE)`
`=VLOOKUP(A2,Prices!A2:C50,2,FALSE)`
`=VLOOKUP(A2,Prices!A2:C50,3,FALSE)`
`=VLOOKUP(Prices!A2:C50,A2,3,FALSE)`

rubric: Price is the third column of A:C and FALSE forces an exact match.
Distractors use approximate match, the wrong column index, or swap the lookup value and the table.

items.prompt: Cells A1 to A5 contain 10, 20, an empty cell, the text "n/a", and 30. What does `=AVERAGE(A1:A5)` return?
rubric: AVERAGE ignores empty and text cells, so it is 60 divided by 3 numbers, which is 20.
12 divides by all five cells and 15 divides by four; 60 is the sum.

items.prompt: A table lists OrderID, Rep and Month. You want a pivot table showing how many orders each rep handled in each month. Which setup does that?

options.label: Rows: Rep; Columns: Month; Values: Sum of OrderID
Rows: Rep; Columns: Month; Values: Count of OrderID
Rows: OrderID; Columns: Rep; Values: Count of Month
Rows: Month; Filters: Rep; Values: Sum of OrderID

rubric: Rep by Month with a count of OrderID gives the number of orders in each cell.
Summing IDs gives a meaningless total, and the other layouts do not cross rep with month.

items.prompt: The range A2:A20 holds the entries "Yes" or "No". Which formulas return the number of cells that contain "Yes"? Select all that apply.

options.label: `=SUMPRODUCT(--(A2:A20="Yes"))`
`=COUNTA(A2:A20)`
`=COUNTIF(A2:A20,"Yes")`
`=COUNT(A2:A20,"Yes")`

rubric: COUNTIF and SUMPRODUCT with a logical test both count matching cells.
COUNT only counts numbers, and COUNTA counts every non-empty cell, including No.

items.prompt: A sales sheet has each rep's monthly sales in B2. Policy says reps earn 5% commission on sales of 10,000 or more, and 2% on anything below that. You are writing the commission formula in C2 to be filled down the column. Which formula applies the policy correctly?
rubric: The test must be >= 10000 and the 5% rate multiplies B2 when true.
Distractors miss exactly 10,000, swap the rates, or return a rate rather than a commission amount.

items.prompt: A VLOOKUP with FALSE as the last argument returns #N/A for ID 1042, yet 1042 clearly appears in the first column of the lookup table. Which cause is most likely?

options.label: The ID in the lookup cell is text while the table holds numbers, so the exact match fails
The table is not sorted ascending by ID, and exact-match lookups need sorted data to work
The column index is larger than the table width, which makes VLOOKUP return #N/A for rows
Calculation is set to manual, so the lookup shows an error until the sheet is recalculated

rubric: A text-versus-number mismatch makes visually identical IDs fail an exact match.
Exact match does not need sorting, an oversized index gives #REF!, and manual calculation shows stale values.

items.prompt: You built a pivot table from A1:D200. Twenty new rows were typed in at rows 201 to 220, and refreshing the pivot does not show them. What is the most likely cause?

options.label: The Values field is set to Count, which ignores rows entered after the pivot was built
A report filter on the pivot hides every row added after its creation date automatically
The pivot's source range still ends at the old last row, so the new rows fall outside it
Pivot tables only read formulas, so typed rows must be converted to formulas first

rubric: A fixed source range means refresh cannot reach rows outside it; extend the range or use a table.
The other options invent behaviours that pivot tables do not have.

items.prompt: Cell D2 holds `=C2/SUM(C2:C10)` and is filled down to D10 to get each row's share of the total. The shares are right in row 2 but wrong from row 3 down. What is the fault?

options.label: The cells need percent formatting, because unformatted values distort the division result
The numerator needs a $ anchor, since C2 must stay fixed while the total range moves
SUM cannot be used inside a division, so the denominator is recalculated as zero
The total range C2:C10 is not anchored, so on fill-down it shifts and omits later rows

rubric: Without $ anchors the SUM range slides down with each row, dropping data and extending past it.
Formatting only changes display, SUM works inside division, and the numerator must stay relative.

items.prompt: A column chart shows regional sales that all fall between 960 and 1,000, yet West looks several times taller than East. Which chart feature most likely causes this impression?

options.label: The vertical axis minimum is set near 950, so the bars' heights exaggerate small gaps
Data labels are switched on, which scales every bar relative to its printed number
Gridlines are too dense, which changes how large each region's total actually is
Column charts cannot compare regions, so the bars distort values and a pie is required

rubric: A truncated axis makes bar height no longer proportional to value, inflating small differences.
Column charts suit comparisons, and labels and gridlines do not rescale bars.

items.prompt: Your company has 85 customers, but a pivot table of Count of Customer over the transactions list shows 120. What explains the gap?

options.label: Count of Customer only counts the first purchase and then repeats it for each region
Count of Customer skips blank cells, so some real customers are missing from the total
Count of Customer adds numeric IDs together, which inflates the figure beyond the rows
Count of Customer counts transaction rows, so repeat customers are counted each time

rubric: Count tallies rows, so customers with several transactions are counted repeatedly; a distinct count is needed.
Skipping blanks would lower the total, and Count does not add IDs.

items.prompt: `=SUMIFS(C2:C100,A2:A100,"West")` returns 0, although many rows visibly show West in column A and amounts in column C. Which are plausible causes? Select all that apply.

options.label: The amounts in column C are stored as text rather than numbers
Column A has been sorted in descending order
The amounts in column C are formatted as currency
Region entries contain trailing spaces, such as "West ", so they do not match

rubric: Trailing spaces break the criteria match and text amounts are ignored by the sum.
Currency formatting and sort order do not affect SUMIFS results.

items.prompt: You filter a sales table to Region = West. A total cell below it uses `=SUM(D2:D500)` and still shows the total for all regions, but your manager wants the total of visible rows only. Why does this happen, and what fixes it?

options.label: SUM only skips rows hidden by hand, not by a filter; wrap the range in COUNTIF so filtered rows are left out of the total
SUM recalculates only when you press F9 after filtering; press it and the total will drop to the visible rows only
The filter was applied to the wrong column; clear it and filter column D instead of Region so the total updates
SUM counts filtered-out rows too; use `=SUBTOTAL(9,D2:D500)`, which skips rows hidden by the filter

rubric: SUM ignores filter state, whereas SUBTOTAL excludes filtered-out rows.
Wrapping in COUNTIF, refiltering a different column, or pressing F9 do not change what SUM includes.

items.prompt: A lookup `=VLOOKUP(A2, Prices!A:B, 2, FALSE)` returns #N/A for product codes like 10432, though 10432 is visibly listed in the Prices sheet. Other codes work. What is the most likely cause?

options.label: The FALSE argument forces a sorted search, which skips some rows
VLOOKUP cannot search a full-column reference such as A:B
Those codes are stored as text in one sheet and as numbers in the other
The Prices table has more than 255 rows, so later codes are missed

rubric: Text-versus-number mismatches make visually identical keys fail an exact match.
Distractors invent limits (sorted search, row counts, full-column references) that do not exist for exact-match VLOOKUP.

items.prompt: A pivot table was built from `Sales!A1:F500`. Last week 40 new rows were typed in rows 501-540. After clicking Refresh, the pivot totals do not change. What explains this?

options.label: Refresh only updates formatting and layout; new values are loaded when the file is next closed and reopened
The pivot's source range still ends at row 500, so the new rows are outside it
Pivot tables only recalculate after the source sheet has been re-sorted, which forces a full cache rebuild
The new rows have dates that pivots exclude until the Date field is grouped by month or year

rubric: A pivot reads a fixed source range unless it is based on a Table or the range is extended.
Refresh re-reads the existing range; it does not grow it.

items.prompt: A column of 100 cells (B2:B101) contains numbers, with some cells showing blank because their formula returns "". A user computes `=SUM(B2:B101)/COUNTA(B2:B101)` and gets a lower figure than `=AVERAGE(B2:B101)`. Why?

options.label: SUM skips every cell that contains a formula, so the numerator is too small
COUNTA counts the "" cells, so the denominator is too large
COUNTA counts only text cells in the range, so the denominator is too small
AVERAGE rounds its result up to the nearest whole number, but SUM does not

rubric: COUNTA counts any non-empty cell, including formulas that return an empty string; AVERAGE ignores text.
Other options misstate how SUM or COUNTA treat formula cells.

items.prompt: A tax of 8% sits in C1. In D2 someone enters `=B2*$C1` and fills it down to D50. Row 2 is right, but later rows give wrong or zero results. What is the fault?

options.label: The dollar sign locks the column but not the row, so only the column letter is protected
The row number is not locked, so it shifts to C2, C3 and so on instead of staying on C1
Fill-down converts cell references to fixed values after the first row has been calculated
The multiplication needs a SUMPRODUCT to work correctly when it is filled over many rows

rubric: With $C1 only the column is locked; the row drifts down on fill. It needs $C$1.
Distractors misread what the dollar sign locks.

items.prompt: A pivot table of order dates from 2023 and 2024 was grouped by Months only. The 'January' row shows a total nearly double any other month's. What is the most likely reason?

options.label: Grouping by Months turns the dates into text labels, so the first month is counted twice
Years were left out of the grouping, so both Januaries merged
Grouping by Months sorts the orders by date, so January shows the running total up to that point
The pivot applied a leap-year adjustment to the first month, so January counted twice

rubric: Grouping by month alone merges the same month across years; add Years to the grouping.
The other options give implausible mechanisms.

items.prompt: A column of imported amounts gives `=SUM(C2:C200)` far below the expected total. Which are plausible causes? Select all that apply.

options.label: Some amounts are stored as text, for example with an apostrophe prefix
Some cells hold non-breaking spaces, so they read as text rather than numbers
The data actually continues to row 230, beyond the summed range
Cells formatted as currency are skipped by SUM unless formatted as General
Rows hidden by a filter are excluded from the SUM total

rubric: Text-numbers, stray spaces and a short range all lower SUM.
SUM includes hidden or filtered rows, and number formats do not affect it.

items.prompt: A workbook of 40,000 rows becomes very slow: every single cell edit freezes it for about 10 seconds. Column E in every row holds `=SUM(INDIRECT("Data!B"&ROW()&":D"&ROW()))`. The file has no pivots or charts. Which is the most likely cause of the slowdown?

options.label: The 40,000 rows exceed what a single worksheet can hold in memory
SUM is slow on three-cell ranges, so it needs SUMPRODUCT
Referencing another sheet always forces a full file reload per edit
INDIRECT is volatile, so all 40,000 formulas recalculate after every edit

rubric: INDIRECT is volatile and recalculates on any change, multiplying the cost across 40,000 rows.
Distractors blame SUM, sheet capacity or cross-sheet references, none of which explain the delay.

items.prompt: A team lookup must (1) survive someone inserting columns in the source table, (2) return exact matches only, and (3) be readable by colleagues. Which formula best meets all three?

options.label: `=VLOOKUP(A2, Src!A:F, 4, FALSE)`, since the exact-match flag is set and the column number 4 is easy for colleagues to read
`=XLOOKUP(A2, Src!A:A, Src!D:D)`, since it names the return column directly and defaults to exact match
`=VLOOKUP(A2, Src!A:F, 4, TRUE)`, since approximate match runs faster on big sorted tables and the index adjusts
`=INDEX(Src!A:F, MATCH(A2, Src!A:A, 1), 4)`, since MATCH type 1 is the standard mode and INDEX tracks columns

rubric: XLOOKUP points at the return column itself, so inserted columns do not break it, and it is exact by default.
VLOOKUP's hard-coded index breaks on insertion; approximate match types fail the exact-only criterion.

items.prompt: Ten colleagues will type department codes into a shared sheet. Criteria: bad entries must be blocked at entry, the allowed list must be editable in one place, and no macros. Which approach is best?

options.label: A COUNTIF check column beside the codes that flags any invalid entry once typing is finished
Data validation: a dropdown tied to a list range, rejecting invalid entries
Conditional formatting that turns any code missing from the list red, so users notice and fix errors
A note pinned at the top of the sheet listing the allowed codes, updated whenever the list changes

rubric: Validation with a list range blocks bad input and centralises the list without macros.
Formatting, notes and check columns detect or advise but do not block.

items.prompt: A monthly summary must keep a fixed layout feeding a dashboard, pick up new source rows automatically, and need no manual refresh step. Which design best meets these criteria?

options.label: A pivot table on a fixed range, which is refreshed by hand each month
`SUMIFS` formulas that reference columns of an Excel Table holding the data
A filtered view of the data, with subtotals added by hand under each group
A copied static table, pasted as values after each month's close

rubric: Table column references grow with new rows and recalculate automatically, keeping the layout fixed.
Pivots need refresh, pasted values go stale, and manual subtotals are fragile.

items.prompt: You must show how three regions' monthly revenue moved over 12 months so readers can compare levels and trends of each region. Which chart best fits?

options.label: A single column chart showing only the annual totals per region
A 3D pie chart per month, with each region as a slice
A line chart with months on the axis and one line per region
A stacked area chart that hides the individual regions' levels

rubric: Lines let readers compare trends and levels across regions over time.
Pies, stacked areas and annual totals hide either the trend or the individual values.

items.prompt: A colleague typed the tax rate `0.2` directly into 500 formulas like `=B2*0.2`. The rate changes yearly, and auditors need to see the assumption. Which fix best meets those needs?

options.label: Round each result to a whole number so that yearly rate changes have less effect on totals
Use find and replace on 0.2 each year, then note the change date in the file's version history
Add a cell comment on the first formula explaining the 0.2 rate and where it came from
Put the rate in one labeled cell and reference it as `$B$1` or a named range

rubric: One labeled input referenced absolutely gives a single update point and a visible assumption.
Find-and-replace can hit unrelated 0.2 values and leaves no visible assumption; comments and rounding do not fix it.

items.prompt: A workbook keeps one tab per month with identical columns, each with a merged title row and blank spacer rows between blocks. Management wants year-wide filtering and pivots. Which are valid criticisms of this design? Select all that apply.

options.label: Splitting same-structure data across tabs makes year-wide pivots and formulas harder
Twelve tabs exceed the maximum number of rows a workbook can hold
Merged titles and blank spacer rows inside the data block break sorting, filtering and pivots
Excel cannot reference cells on other worksheets, so tab totals are impossible

rubric: One consistent table with a month column supports pivots and filters; merged cells and blank rows disrupt data ranges.
Cross-sheet references and row limits are not real obstacles here.

items.prompt: In Google Sheets, five regional managers must update only their own region's rows in a shared sales tracker, while finance sees all regions. Criteria: keep a single source of truth, prevent accidental overwriting of others' rows, and avoid manual merging. Which approach is best?

options.label: Keep one sheet and protect each region's rows so only that manager edits them
Email each manager a copy, then paste their returned rows into the master sheet
Create one tab per manager, then have finance copy every tab into a totals sheet
Give everyone edit access and rely on version history to undo any mistakes later

rubric: Protected ranges on a single sheet keep one source and block edits to others' rows without merging.
Copies and per-manager tabs require manual merging; version history only repairs mistakes after they occur.

items.prompt: A sheet has 300,000 unsorted rows with unique text IDs. Each of 50,000 report rows must return 8 columns by exact ID, and recalculation time matters. Which approach is the best trade-off?

options.label: Run MATCH once per report row in a helper column, then INDEX that row number for each of the 8 columns
Write one exact-match VLOOKUP per output column, which keeps each cell independent and simple to audit later on
Wrap each lookup in IFERROR after a COUNTIF check, so each cell confirms the ID exists before it looks it up
Sort the data and use approximate-match VLOOKUP, since binary search is faster and usually returns the same result

rubric: One MATCH per row replaces 8 full searches, so it cuts calculation cost and keeps exact matching.
Approximate match on sorted data can return wrong rows for missing IDs, and COUNTIF adds another scan per cell.

items.prompt: A colleague replaces a labelled tax-rate cell with the constant in 4,000 formulas, such as `=B2*1.0825`, claiming it makes the workbook faster. Which critique is best?

options.label: Valid only if formulas are filled down from one cell, because fill keeps all 4,000 copies of the constant identical
Invalid: the speed gain is negligible, and the hidden constant means 4,000 formulas need editing when the rate changes
Valid: constants calculate noticeably faster than cell references, so documenting the rate in a note is enough
Invalid: each row should carry its own copy of the rate in a column so that rows can be edited separately

rubric: Reference lookups cost almost nothing, while hard-coded assumptions are hidden and costly to change and audit.
Per-row copies of the rate still spread the assumption across thousands of cells.

items.prompt: A workbook uses OFFSET and INDIRECT to define growing ranges and now recalculates slowly on every edit. Criteria: ranges must grow with new rows, recalculation must drop, and formulas must stay live. Which fix is best?

options.label: Set calculation to manual permanently, so the volatile functions stop recalculating until someone presses F9
Convert the data to a Table or use INDEX-based ranges, since these grow with data and are not volatile
Replace every range with a fixed reference to row 100000, which avoids volatility and still covers future rows
Paste the current results as values each month, which removes all volatile formulas and keeps the numbers stable

rubric: Tables or INDEX ranges expand automatically without recalculating on every change.
Manual calc, oversized fixed ranges and pasted values each lose either liveness, reliability or accuracy.

items.prompt: You must chart monthly revenue for a product line (about 5,000,000) and a pilot line (about 40,000) so that a board can compare their growth rates honestly. Which choice is best?

options.label: Index both series to 100 at the first month on one axis, so growth rates are comparable without distorted scales
Plot the pilot on a secondary axis scaled to fill the chart, so its movement is as visible as the main line
Plot both as stacked columns, so the combined height shows total revenue and each segment shows its share
Plot both on one axis in raw dollars, because the true scale shows how small the pilot is relative to the main line

rubric: Indexing shows relative growth on a common axis, which is what the board is comparing.
Dual axes are arbitrary and misleading; raw scale hides the pilot's trend; stacking obscures growth.

items.prompt: A pivot table shows 'Average of Unit Price' by region, but orders vary from 1 to 5,000 units. The goal is the average price actually realised per unit. Which judgement is correct?

options.label: Use Median of Unit Price instead, since it handles the wide spread in order sizes and removes the distortion
Keep the Average of Unit Price field, since the average of order prices is the standard realised price per unit
Add a calculated field Revenue/Units, since this weights each order by volume, unlike a plain average of prices
Weight by adding a Count of Orders field next to the average, so readers can mentally adjust for order size

rubric: Total revenue divided by total units gives a volume-weighted price; averaging order prices treats 1 unit like 5,000.
Median still ignores volume, and adding a count leaves the figure itself unweighted.

items.prompt: A report uses `=VLOOKUP(A2,Data!A:D,4,FALSE)` to fetch a value. Which are genuine weaknesses of this design? Select all that apply.

options.label: The lookup key must be in the leftmost column, so reshaping the table can force a rewrite of the formula
Inserting a column inside A:D changes which field the hard-coded index 4 returns, without any visible error
FALSE forces the data to be sorted ascending, so unsorted tables return unreliable results for exact matches
Keys stored as text in one sheet and numbers in the other return #N/A even when they look identical

rubric: Index numbers, leftmost-key rule and text/number mismatches are real fragilities of VLOOKUP.
FALSE means exact match and requires no sorting; the sorted requirement applies to TRUE.

items.prompt: A shared budget workbook has six editors. Last month someone typed over a total formula with a number, and nobody noticed until the board meeting. Criteria: inputs must stay editable, formulas must be protected, and changes must be traceable. Which control is best?

options.label: Hide the formula columns so editors cannot see them, and save a pasted-values backup of the whole sheet at each month end
Lock and protect the formula cells, leave input cells unlocked, and use version history to trace changes
Email all editors a reminder not to type in formula cells, and ask each of them to check the totals before every board meeting
Give edit rights to one person who enters everyone's data, so that a single owner is accountable for every cell in the workbook

rubric: Protection blocks overwriting formulas while inputs stay open, and version history shows who changed what.
Reminders and hiding do not prevent edits; a single editor fails the editable-inputs criterion.

items.prompt: A price log Log has columns Product, Date, Price, unsorted, with many rows per product. Design one cell formula, no helper columns, that returns the most recent price for the product in A2.

options.label: `=INDEX(Log[Price],MATCH(A2,Log[Product],0))`
`=MAXIFS(Log[Price],Log[Product],A2)`
`=VLOOKUP(A2,Log,3,TRUE)`
`=LOOKUP(2,1/((Log[Product]=A2)*(Log[Date]=MAXIFS(Log[Date],Log[Product],A2))),Log[Price])`

rubric: It finds the latest date for the product, then returns the price on the row matching both product and date.
INDEX/MATCH returns the first row, MAXIFS on price returns the highest price, and approximate VLOOKUP needs sorted keys.

items.prompt: Scores sit in B2:B100 and contain ties. Design a rank in C2, filled down, giving each row a unique rank 1 to n, with the earlier row winning ties. Which formula meets this?

options.label: `=RANK(B2,B$2:B$100)+COUNTIF(B$2:B2,B2)-1`

rubric: The expanding COUNTIF range adds 0 for the first tie, 1 for the second and so on, giving unique ranks in row order.
Plain RANK and COUNTIF with a fixed range leave ties or push them to the same offset.

items.prompt: Transactions have Customer in A and Amount in B, in any order and re-sortable. Design C2, filled down, so it shows each customer's running total up to that row, still correct after re-sorting.
rubric: An expanding SUMIF adds only the same customer's amounts above and including the row, regardless of grouping.
The IF version needs grouped rows; SUM ignores customers; a fixed range gives the full total.

items.prompt: A dashboard design: data in A1:F5000, a month dropdown in H1, tiles using `=SUMIFS($F$2:$F$5000,$A$2:$A$5000,H1)`. Rows are appended weekly and the tiles must stay correct with no maintenance. What does the design lack?

options.label: Frozen panes on the header row of the data, so appended rows are displayed correctly beneath the headers
Volatile TODAY() calls in every tile, so each tile recalculates itself whenever new rows are appended
A macro that rewrites the range references each Monday, so the formulas always reflect the current last row
A Table or whole-column references as the data source, so appended rows are automatically included in every tile

rubric: Fixed ranges stop at row 5000, so new rows would be ignored; Tables or full-column references expand.
Macros add maintenance, TODAY does not extend ranges, and frozen panes affect display only.

items.prompt: Tasks are in A2:F500 with due date in C and status in D. Design one conditional formatting rule to shade the whole row when the due date is past and status is not Done. Which rule and range work?

options.label: `=AND(C2<TODAY(),D2<>"Done")` applied to A2:F500
`=AND($C2<TODAY(),$D2<>"Done")` applied to C2 only
`=AND($C2<TODAY(),$D2<>"Done")` applied to A2:F500
`=OR($C2<TODAY(),$D2<>"Done")` applied to A2:F500

rubric: Column-anchored references with AND test both conditions for every cell in the row.
Unanchored columns shift across the range, OR fires too often, and a single-cell range shades only that cell.

items.prompt: You are building a reusable annual budget template that others will fill in. It must have no hidden assumptions, resist accidental damage and reject bad entries. Which design elements belong in it? Select all that apply.

options.label: Protection on formula cells, with input cells left unlocked so users can fill the template in
Data validation on input cells, such as numeric limits and dropdown lists, to reject out-of-range entries
A dedicated inputs sheet with labelled named cells that every formula references instead of typed constants
Merged cells spanning each section's columns, to keep headings tidy and ranges easy to sort and filter

rubric: Named inputs, validation and protection address hidden assumptions, bad entries and accidental damage.
Merged cells interfere with sorting, filtering and fills, so they do not belong.

items.prompt: A sales commission is marginal: 2% on the first 10,000, 3% on 10,000 to 50,000, 5% above 50,000. Tier floors are in F2:F4 (0, 10000, 50000) and incremental rates in H2:H4 (2%, 1%, 2%). Sales are in B2. Design one formula that stays correct when the table is edited.

options.label: `=VLOOKUP(B2,F2:H4,3,TRUE)*B2`

rubric: Each tier adds its incremental rate on the portion above its floor, which sums to the marginal commission and reads from the table.
VLOOKUP and nested IF apply one rate to all sales and the last option applies incremental rates to the full amount.
